text.title: Trend Analysis Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules that separate a trend scan from a horoscope: every trend carries a measured rate of change, an expiry date, a pre-named disconfirming signal, three non-shared sources, and an implication that names the decision it flips.

rule.statement: Each entry in `trends` MUST carry a metric, a t0 value with date, a t1 value with date, and the source of the series. A directional statement with no measured magnitude ("AI adoption is accelerating") is a theme, not a trend, and is cut from the artefact.
rule.rationale: A theme cannot be wrong, so the next review cannot score it and the scan never accumulates a track record; a rate makes the claim checkable at the next re-measurement, which is the only mechanism by which a forecasting artefact ever improves.

rule.statement: Every trend carries its own `valid_until` date — the point at which its rate must be re-measured — set no later than the artefact's `horizon_months` and shorter for faster-moving series. A trend cited past its `valid_until` is treated as unsourced.
rule.rationale: A single artefact-level horizon expires all claims at once, but trends inside one scan move at different speeds; without per-trend expiry the slow-moving regulatory item and the fast-moving pricing item are quoted with equal confidence eighteen months later, when only one of them is still true.

rule.statement: Each trend MUST name the observation that would falsify it: a specific metric, a threshold, and where it is published. The disconfirmer is fixed at authoring time and MUST NOT be rewritten at review time to fit what happened.

rationale.source: Schwartz, The Art of the Long View — early-warning indicators; Popperian falsifiability

rule.rationale: Without a pre-committed disconfirmer, every subsequent outcome gets narrated as consistent with the trend, so the scan can never be shown wrong; that is the exact property that makes horoscopes feel accurate and makes trend reports un-improvable.

rule.statement: `signals_per_trend` requires ≥3 signals that do not share a primary source — three articles quoting the same analyst report count as one. At least one signal MUST be a hard series (price, volume, headcount, filings, procurement or regulatory calendar), not commentary.
rule.rationale: Media coverage is autocorrelated: outlets cite each other, so counting articles measures how loudly a trend was reported, and that volume peaks when the asset or the idea is most over-priced — the count is a contrarian indicator being read as a confirming one.

rule.statement: Each entry in `implications` MUST name (a) the first-order effect it descends from, (b) which of our decisions changes — price, roadmap item, hiring, channel, build-vs-buy, and (c) the direction of the change. An implication that restates the trend in different words is rejected.
rule.rationale: Restated implications leave the artefact with nothing to act on, so it is filed and never consulted; an artefact that is never consulted is also never tested against outcomes, and its errors persist into the next scan unchallenged.

rule.statement: `horizon_months` (12-24) MUST be greater than the publication lag of the slowest cited signal, and each signal records its field date separately from its publication date. A trend evidenced only by annually published survey data requires at least one higher-frequency leading indicator before it can support a 12-month claim.

rationale.source: Internal — signal-latency check on annual industry surveys

rule.rationale: Annual surveys are published months after their field window closes, so at authoring time a meaningful share of the horizon has already elapsed against data that describes the past; the forecast is then made about a period that partially already happened.

rule.statement: Do NOT run when (a) the decision executes inside the current quarter — a 12-24 month read cannot change it; route to market-analysis for a current-state view; (b) no time series exists in the domain, only opinion pieces — rule `three-signals-not-three-citations-of-one` cannot be satisfied; (c) the domain's cadence is faster than your review cycle, where a periodic scan is structurally stale — route to a continuous monitoring setup; (d) the intended use is narrative for a pitch rather than a decision input.
rule.rationale: Each case produces an artefact whose `signals_per_trend` and `valid_until` fields can only be filled with plausible fiction, and a fictional trend scan is more damaging than none because it is quoted with the authority of the format.
